questions.question: What does $\operatorname{span}(v_1,\ldots,v_k)$ contain?
options: Only the scalar coefficients used in combinations.

questions.question: If $w\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2)$, what does this mean?
options: $w$ must be perpendicular to both $v_1$ and $v_2$.
$w$ must be equal to either $v_1$ or $v_2$.
$w$ is a scalar rather than a vector.
There are scalars $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with $w=\alpha v_1+\beta v_2$.

questions.question: What is the span of one nonzero vector in $\mathbb R^2$?
options: A line not passing through the origin.

questions.question: When does a collection of vectors span a vector space $V$?
options: When the collection has exactly two vectors.
When the collection contains no zero vector.

questions.question: Among all subspaces of $V$ that contain $v_1,\dots,v_k$, the span $\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ is:
What is $\operatorname{span}((1,0),(0,1))$ in $\mathbb R^2$?
Is $(3,4)$ in $\operatorname{span}((1,0),(0,1))$?
options: No, because spans contain only unit vectors.
No, because $(3,4)$ is not one of the listed vectors.

questions.question: Can the span of a single nonzero vector $v$ ever equal all of $\mathbb R^2$?
options: No, one vector spans at most a line
Only if $v$ is a unit vector

questions.question: What is $\operatorname{span}(\,)$ of the empty list (no vectors)?
Is $(1,0)$ in $\operatorname{span}((1,1))$?
options: Yes, because every vector in $\mathbb R^2$ lies in the span of one nonzero vector.
No, because every scalar multiple of $(1,1)$ has equal coordinates.
No, because spans cannot contain nonzero vectors.

questions.question: Why is the span of a collection of vectors itself a vector space?
options: Linear combinations are closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
A span is a vector space only when the vectors are orthogonal.
A span always contains exactly one vector.
A span is defined by removing scalar coefficients.

questions.question: What happens to the span if a vector already in the span of the others is added to the list?
options: The span stops being a vector space.

questions.question: Can two different lists of vectors have the same span?
options: Only if the lists are written in the same order, in all instances without exception.
Only if all vectors in both lists are zero.
No, the span determines the list uniquely.
Yes, different generating lists can reach the same set of vectors.

questions.question: What is $\operatorname{span}((1,0),(1,1))$ in $\mathbb R^2$?
What is $\operatorname{span}((1,1),(2,2))$ in $\mathbb R^2$?
If $v_3=v_1+v_2$, what is $\operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2,v_3)$?
options: A set that cannot contain $v_1$ or $v_2$

questions.question: If two collections have the same span, must they contain the same vectors?
options: Yes, equality of spans forces equality of the lists.
No, they may generate the same set in different ways.
Yes, if the vector space is $\mathbb R^2$.
No, because spans never contain the listed vectors.

questions.question: Why must the zero vector lie in the span of any non-empty collection?
options: It is true only for bases.
Take the largest vector in the list.

questions.question: Is $(1,2,3)$ in $\operatorname{span}((1,0,0),(0,1,0))$ in $\mathbb R^3$?
options: No, because every vector in the span has third coordinate $0$.
No, because spans cannot include vectors in $\mathbb R^3$.
Yes, because two vectors always span $\mathbb R^3$.
Yes, because the first two coordinates can be matched.
